custom.eventDescription:
Documentation which may be relevant to submit, but which is not a minimum requirement, as
not all applicants are in possession of this type of documentation are the following: 

  • Other existing medical documentation, such as medical certificates, specialist medical reports (e.g. from an
    occupational injury case) or neuropsychological assessments regarding your functional impairment,
    which you may possess.
  • If you have been involved in a programme run by the local authority, there may be relevant medical information from this, e.g. programme descriptions from other providers, work trials and/or medical certificates.
  • If, for example, you have been in contact with the local authority in connection with sick leave from your job or have been on a programme, including educational support, income support or a resource programme, descriptions of your functional level will likely have been drawn up, to which you have access. These may also include medical certificates obtained in connection with your  programme, or if you have been on a work trial.
  • If you have been on sick leave from their previous or current workplace, a medical certificate will likely have been issued to your employer, which you may also enclose with your application.

The supporting documentation to be submitted at the time of application must, as a minimum, include medical records
from either the your general practitioner, a specialist, a hospital or an outpatient clinic. 

  

The documentation must describe the your permanent disability.

Documentation specified as a minimum requirement is documentation which you
can obtain themselves free of charge. This comprises:
1) Medical records, including discharge summaries and referrals from you GP, if you
have been or are currently receiving treatment at a public hospital. You can
obtain this documentation from sundhed.dk.
2) Medical records from consultations with your own GP. As a general rule, you
are entitled to access this documentation.
3) Medical records from private hospitals and specialist doctors, if you have been or are currently
receiving treatment at a private hospital or from a specialist doctor. As a general rule, you have the right of access to this documentation.

The required documentation also depends on whether you are in ongoing treatment.
As your treatment is finished, your documentation should also include an a discharge summary or letter of completion.
In this case, you may not have letters of discharge or letters of completion of treatment, which is too be expected and not a problem.

When applying for a disability allowance, you must, at the time of application, enclose
documentation in the form of medical information showing that you have a permanent
disability that may entitle you to a disability allowance, together with a description of this

In addition, you must enclose medical information describing your
diagnostic and treatment history. It is important that you submit all
relevant and up-to-date documentation that describes in detail and comprehensively your
disability.


‘Up-to-date and comprehensive documentation’ means:
1) Tyour diagnosis (if one has been made)
2) A description of the course of the illness and treatment
3) How the illness or disability manifests itself/affects your
day-to-day functioning
4) What treatment you are receiving
5) What treatment is planned (if any)
6) How your illness or disability affects your ability to work (if
possible)


The above information must be submitted if you have it available via your medical records
or other existing medical documentation.

Medical documentation is not, for example, regarded as detailed and comprehensive if you merely
submit:

  • a statement from your own GP, psychiatrist, etc., which merely confirms a diagnosis
  • a medication card showing that you are receiving medication for an illness; or
  • a record from the jobcentre without medical information.
  • a decision, e.g. from the Labour Market Insurance Scheme, SPS, etc., without medical information.

Applications where the above applies will be rejected by the agency without substantive consideration, as
the minimum documentation requirements have not been met. 


A suspected diagnosis will not, in itself, be sufficient as medical documentation,
unless descriptions of symptoms that impair functional capacity are submitted, even if a diagnosis has not yet been made.
As a general rule, a statement from a psychologist cannot stand alone, but it may form part of the assessment.
of the application if, for example, it is supported by a statement from a specialist in psychiatry or other
medical documentation.

If your disability stems from a (previous) accident or similar event,
you must ascertain whether the disability is permanent.
As a general rule, an applicant is not entitled to a disability allowance if an illness, injury
or disability is not already permanent or chronic at the time of its onset.

A disability which, by definition, is not permanent may be assessed as permanent if it lasts for approximately one year.

At the time of application, you must submit the most recent medical information,
which describes your diagnostic and treatment history as well as current symptoms and challenges.


If you are undergoing treatment following an accident or trauma, and the Agency cannot definitively determine the impact at the time of the decision, the Agency may award a time-limited disability
allowance.


It should be noted that, in the event of a refusal on the grounds that the functional impairment is not deemed to be permanent, you may be referred to the option of applying for additional credits as a supplement to the framework
and the support period on grounds of illness.

If you consider applying for a disability allowance on the basis of a congenital disability, you are probably diagnosed and treated during childhood or early adolescence, and you might not have recent medical documentation describing your current level of functioning.

In such cases, it is particularly
important for you to submit medical information regarding your medical history, as well as the most recent
medical records relating to the disability.

In your personal statement, you may describe your situation so that the agency can gain a better understanding of the impact
the disability has.


Congenital disabilities include, for example:

  • Cerebral palsy
  • Muscular dystrophy
  • Intellectual disability
  • Autism spectrum disorder
  • Congenital blindness or visual impairment
  • Severe hearing impairment or deafness

The above list is not exhaustive.
If you have a congenital disability, it is important that you
submit, at the time of application, the most recent medical information describing your diagnostic and treatment history, as well as any current symptoms.

This may include, for example, discharge summaries,
medical records detailing the medical history, including the challenges faced by you
as well as any recent decisions regarding, for example, the granting of housing support, a contact person, a mentor or assistive devices, or
descriptions of any support measures that have been implemented during previous courses of study or at previous workplaces. 

 

If there is no supporting documentation for this, you can include it in your personal statement.
